edits.old: The resulting 1.3B-parameter phi-1 reached **50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval** after 4 days on 8 A100s, ahead of open models ten times its size ([arXiv:2306.11644](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11644)).
edits.new: The resulting 1.3B-parameter phi-1 reached **50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval** after under 4 days of pretraining on 8 A100s plus 7 hours of fine-tuning on ~180M tokens of synthetic exercises (the pretrained base scored 29%), ahead of every open model ten times its size except WizardCoder 16B (57.3%) ([arXiv:2306.11644](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.11644) (Gunasekar et al., 2023-06, preprint)).
edits.why: PDF p.1-3 and Table 1: 50.6% is after fine-tuning on the ~180M-token CodeExercises set (phi-1-base = 29%), fine-tuning added 7 hours to the <4-day pretraining; Table 1 lists WizardCoder 16B at 57.3% HumanEval, above phi-1, so 'ahead of open models ten times its size' is overstated. Also adds the preprint date to the citation.

doubts: The old string (full sentence) is verified unique in 11-applications.md.

row: | | Morris et al., *How Much Do Language Models Memorize?* (2025 ⚑): GPT-style models up to 20M parameters trained on random bitstrings stored about 3.6 bits per parameter; on deduplicated text they memorized until that capacity filled, then generalized, with double descent at that point; a fitted law puts loss-based membership inference at chance beyond ~100 tokens per parameter, validated only on GPT-2 models up to 1.5B and only for a loss-threshold attack | [2505.24832](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.24832) | ✓ [morris-2025-how-much-do-language-models.pdf](sources/morris-2025-how-much-do-language-models.pdf) | [02](notes/02-training-and-adapting.md#pretraining) |
